title: Given a string s and a pattern p, find the start indices of all substrings of s that are anagrams of p. Solve it with the fixed-size sliding window pattern and demonstrate with a complete banking mini-project.
shortTitle: Challenge 2: String Anagrams (Find All Anagram Start Indices)

s1_definition.profdef: This problem asks for every start index in a source string s where a substring of length equal to the pattern p is an anagram of p, meaning it contains exactly the same characters with the same counts in any order. It is solved with a fixed-size sliding window of width equal to the pattern length, maintaining a window count signature compared to the pattern signature via a matched counter, and collecting the start index each time the counts align. It runs in linear time.
s1_definition.analogy: At the National Bank of India, compliance has a required combination of transaction flags for a suspicious pattern, say two cash flags and one wire flag, in any order. They scan a long chronological flag stream for an account and want every position where a block of exactly that size matches the suspicious combination, because each match marks a window to investigate. They slide a fixed-width window and jot down the start index of every matching block.
s1_definition.oneliner: Slide a fixed-width window the size of the pattern and collect every start index where the window's counts match the pattern's counts.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** This problem asks for every start index in a source string s where a substring of length equal to the pattern p is an anagram of p, meaning it contains exactly the same characters with the same counts in any order. It is solved with a fixed-size sliding window of width equal to the pattern length, maintaining a window count signature compared to the pattern signature via a matched counter, and collecting the start index each time the counts align. It runs in linear time.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** At the National Bank of India, compliance has a required combination of transaction flags for a suspicious pattern, say two cash flags and one wire flag, in any order. They scan a long chronological flag stream for an account and want every position where a block of exactly that size matches the suspicious combination, because each match marks a window to investigate. They slide a fixed-width window and jot down the start index of every matching block.

**One line to remember:** Slide a fixed-width window the size of the pattern and collect every start index where the window's counts match the pattern's counts.

sections.s2_technical:
This problem is the all-matches sibling of the permutation-in-a-string question. The difference is that instead of returning true on the first match, we record every start index where the window is an anagram of the pattern. We build a count signature of the pattern, usually an `int[26]` for lowercase letters, and a matching window count of the first p-length characters of the source.

We then slide the window one position at a time across the source. On each slide, one character enters on the right and one character leaves on the left, and we update the window count accordingly. We use the same matched-counter bookkeeping as in the permutation problem: a counter that tracks how many distinct characters currently have exactly their required count. When a character's window count reaches the required amount we increment the counter, and when it moves past the required amount in either direction we decrement, with the mirror updates applied when a character leaves. For example on entry `if (++window[c] == need[c]) matches++; else if (window[c] == need[c] + 1) matches--;`.

Whenever the matched counter equals the number of distinct required characters, the current window is an anagram of the pattern, and we add its start index, which is the right pointer minus the window width plus one, to our result list. We do not stop; we continue sliding to the end to collect all matches. The senior-level nuance is that because we collect indices rather than substrings, and because each slide is constant work thanks to the matched counter, the algorithm stays linear even when there are many matches.

The time complexity is linear, O(s + p), as we build the pattern signature once and perform constant work per slide across the source. The space complexity is O(alphabet size) for the two count structures, plus the output list whose size is the number of matches. This is the standard pattern for collecting all anagram occurrences and is a direct extension of the fixed-size window template.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — At the National Bank of India, the anti-money-laundering team defines suspicious activity as a specific combination of transaction-type flags occurring together in a short consecutive block, regardless of order, for example two cash-deposit flags and one wire-transfer flag within three consecutive transactions. For each account they store a chronological flag stream. The team wants the start index of every consecutive block that matches the suspicious combination, because each such block is a window an investigator must review. This is exactly the find-all-anagrams problem.

Problem 2 — Re-counting each possible block from scratch is wasteful at the bank's transaction volume. The fixed-size window with a matched counter gives constant work per slide and collects all matches in a single linear pass, which keeps the AML screening job fast even on busy accounts.

The code has the shared `Account` class, an `AmlPatternScanner` service with a `findSuspiciousBlockStarts` method implementing the fixed window collecting all start indices, and a runnable `FindAnagramsDemo` main class that scans Rajesh's and Priya's flag streams for the suspicious combination, logging each match at fine level and the final list of start indices at info level.

sections.s5_journey:
Input data: Rajesh's flag stream "CCWCCW" with combo "CCW", which needs two C and one W, two distinct requirements. The window width is 3. We keep a window count map and a matches counter at 0.

Step 1: Right at index 0, C. Window C becomes 1, required 2, not equal, matches stays 0.

Step 2: Right at index 1, C. Window C becomes 2, equals required 2, matches becomes 1.

Step 3: Right at index 2, W. Window W becomes 1, equals required 1, matches becomes 2, equal to the two requirements. Block indices 0 to 2, "CCW", matches, so we record start index 0.

Step 4: Right at index 3, C. Window C becomes 3. Also the element leaving is index 0, a C, so window C drops to 2. Entering made C exceed then leaving brought it back; the net is window C stays at 2, W at 1, matches stays 2. Block indices 1 to 3, "CWC", matches again, record start index 1? Let us trace carefully. Actually "CWC" has two C and one W, which is a valid anagram of "CCW", so start index 1 is recorded.

Step 5: Right at index 4, C. Entering C: window C becomes 3, exceeds required, matches drops to 1. Leaving index 1, a C: window C drops to 2, back to required, matches becomes 2. Block indices 2 to 4, "WCC", two C one W, matches, record start index 2.

Step 6: Right at index 5, W. Entering W: window W becomes 2, exceeds required 1, matches drops to 1. Leaving index 2, a W: window W drops to 1, back to required, matches becomes 2. Block indices 3 to 5, "CCW", matches, record start index 3.

Every length-three block of "CCWCCW" turns out to be an anagram of "CCW", so the recorded starts are 0, 1, 2, and 3.

sections.s5b_flow:
```
  Input: flags "CCWCCW", combo "CCW" (need C:2, W:1, distinct=2), width=3
    │
    ▼
  AmlPatternScanner.findSuspiciousBlockStarts()
    │ window={}, matches=0, starts=[]
    │
    ├─ r=0 'C' winC1 matches0
    ├─ r=1 'C' winC2=need matches1
    ├─ r=2 'W' winW1=need matches2 block[0..2]"CCW" → start 0
    ├─ r=3 'C' in C(→3) out C@0(→2) matches2 block[1..3]"CWC" → start 1
    ├─ r=4 'C' in C(→3 matches--) out C@1(→2 matches++) block[2..4] → start 2
    └─ r=5 'W' in W(→2 matches--) out W@2(→1 matches++) block[3..5] → start 3
    │
    ▼
  Output: [0, 1, 2, 3]  (all consecutive blocks that match the AML combo)
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
This problem asks for the start indices of every substring of a source string that is an anagram of a pattern, and I solve it with a fixed-size sliding window of width equal to the pattern length, running in linear time. I build a count signature of the pattern and slide a window of exactly that width across the source. A block is an anagram precisely when its character counts match the pattern's counts, so I detect those matches efficiently and record the start index of every one, continuing all the way to the end rather than stopping at the first.

To make each slide constant work I use the matched-counter technique: a counter of how many distinct required characters currently have exactly the right amount in the window. When a character enters I update that counter on the exact crossing of the required count, and when a character leaves the window I apply the mirror update. Whenever the counter equals the number of distinct required characters, the window is an anagram and I add its start index to the result list. Because I collect indices rather than copying substrings, and each slide is constant time, the whole scan stays linear even with many matches.

In my banking project at the National Bank of India I used this on the anti-money-laundering team. We defined suspicious activity as a specific combination of transaction-type flags occurring together in a short consecutive block regardless of order, and for each account we stored a chronological flag stream. We collected the start index of every consecutive block that matched the suspicious combination, because each one was a window an investigator had to review. The fixed window with a matched counter gave constant work per slide and gathered all matches in a single linear pass, keeping the screening job fast even on high-volume accounts.

The senior-level point I make is that this is the all-occurrences extension of the permutation-in-a-string problem, differing only in that I collect every match instead of returning on the first, which shows I understand how one window template generalizes across a family of questions. I also mention that for a fixed alphabet I would use integer arrays instead of hash maps to remove boxing overhead, and that in production I run this as a streaming computation over each account's flag events so suspicious blocks surface in near real time rather than in a nightly batch. Framing the solution as both a reusable template and a streaming pipeline is what signals real experience to an interviewer.
